{{short description|Formula to quantify column buckling under a given load}}
[[File:FIG2.png|thumb|294x294px|''Fig. 1: Critical stress vs slenderness ratio for steel, for E = 200{{nbsp}}GPa, yield strength = 240{{nbsp}}MPa''.]]

'''Euler's critical load''' or '''Euler's buckling load''' is the compressive [[Structural load|load]] at which a slender [[column]] will suddenly bend or [[Buckling |buckle]]. It is given by the formula:<ref>{{Cite web|title=Column Buckling {{!}} MechaniCalc |url=https://mechanicalc.com/reference/column-buckling|access-date=2020-12-27|website=mechanicalc.com}}</ref>

<math display="block">P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{(KL)^2}</math>

where
*<math>P_{cr}</math>, Euler's critical load (longitudinal compression load on column),
*<math>E</math>, [[Young's modulus]] of the column material,
*<math>I</math>, minimum [[second moment of area]] of the cross section of the column (area moment of inertia),
*<math>L</math>, unsupported [[length]] of column,
*<math>K</math>, [[:File:ColumnEffectiveLength.png|column effective length factor]]

This formula was derived in [[1744]] by the [[Switzerland|Swiss]] [[mathematician]] [[Leonhard Euler]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Euler |first1=Leonard |title=Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas maximi minimive proprietate gaudentes sive solutio problematis isoperimetrici latissimo sensu accepti |trans-title=A method of finding curved lines enjoying the maximum-minimum property, or the solution of the isoperimetric problem in the broadest sense |date=1744 |publisher=Marc Michel Bousquet et Cie. |location=Geneva, Switzerland |pages=267-268 |url=https://archive.org/details/methodusinvenie00eule/page/266/mode/2up |language=Latin}}  From pp. 267-268:  ''"37.  Quae ante de specie prima sunt annotata inservire possunt viribus columnarum dijudicandis. […] contra vero si pondus P fuerit majus, columna incurvationi resistere non poterit."'' (37. Those [things] which have been noted before about the first type can serve in judging the strength of columns. So let the column AB be placed vertically on the base A, bearing the load P.  For if the column is already arranged in such a way that it cannot slide [away] from the load P, [then] if [the load] will have been too great, there will be nothing else to fear except the bending of the column; in this case, therefore, the column may be regarded as endowed with elasticity.  Therefore let the absolute elasticity of the column = E''kk'', and its height AB = 2''f'' = ''a''; and [in] §25 above [p. 261] we have seen that the required bending force on this column or the minimum [load that is required to bend this column] = ππ E''kk''/4''ff'' = ππ E''kk''/''aa''.  Thus, unless the load P being carried is greater than E''kk''/''aa'', absolutely no bending will have to be feared; but on the other hand, if the load P will have been greater, the column will not be able to resist bending.)</ref> The column will remain straight for loads less than the critical load. The ''critical load'' is the greatest load that will not cause lateral deflection (buckling). For loads greater than the critical load, the column will deflect laterally. The critical load puts the column in a state of [[Instability|unstable]] equilibrium. A load beyond the critical load causes the column to [[Structural integrity and failure|fail]] by [[buckling]]. As the load is increased beyond the critical load the lateral deflections increase, until it may fail in other modes such as yielding of the material. Loading of columns beyond the critical load are not addressed in this article.

[[Johnson's parabolic formula]], an alternative used for low slenderness ratios was constructed by John Butler Johnson (1850–1902) in 1893.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://asmedigitalcollection.asme.org/astm-ebooks/book/1045/Test-Methods-for-Compression-Members |title=Test Methods for Compression Members |date=1967-01-01 |publisher=ASTM International |isbn=978-0-8031-6174-0 |editor-last=Committee E-1 |location=100 Barr Harbor Drive, PO Box C700, West Conshohocken, PA 19428-2959 |language=en |doi=10.1520/stp419-eb}}</ref>

== Assumptions of the model ==
[[File:ColumnEffectiveLength.png|thumb|343x343px|''Fig. 2: Column effective length factors for Euler's critical load. In practical design, it is recommended to increase the factors as shown above.'']]

The following assumptions are made while deriving Euler's formula:<ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-03-28|title=Twelve Viva Questions on Columns and Struts|url=http://engineering.myindialist.com/2015/twelve-viva-questions-on-columns-and-struts/|access-date=2020-12-27|website=Engineering Tutorials|language=en}}</ref>
# The [[material]] of the column is homogeneous and [[Isotropy|isotropic]].
# The compressive load on the column is axial only.
# The column is free from initial [[stress (mechanics)|stress]].
# The [[weight]] of the column is neglected.
# The column is initially straight (no eccentricity of the axial load).
# Pin joints are [[friction]]-less (no moment constraint) and fixed ends are rigid (no rotation deflection).
# The [[Cross section (geometry)|cross-section]] of the column is uniform throughout its length.
# The direct stress is very small as compared to the [[bending]] stress (the material is compressed only within the elastic range of strains).
# The length of the column is very large as compared to the cross-sectional dimensions of the column. 
# The column fails only by buckling. This is true if the compressive stress in the column does not exceed the [[yield strength]] <math>\sigma_y</math> (see figure 1): <math display="block">\sigma = \frac{P_{cr}}{A} = \frac{\pi^2E}{(L_e/r)^2} < \sigma_y</math> where:
#* <math display="inline">{L_e}/{r}</math> is the slenderness ratio,
#* <math>L_e = KL</math> is the effective length,
#* <math display="inline">r = \sqrt{I / A}</math> is the [[radius of gyration]],
#* <math>I</math> is the second moment of area (area moment of inertia),
#* <math>A</math> is the area cross section.

For slender columns, the critical buckling stress is usually lower than the yield stress. In contrast, a stocky column can have a critical buckling stress higher than the yield, i.e. it yields prior to buckling.

== Mathematical derivation ==
=== Pin ended column ===

The following model applies to columns simply supported at each end (<math>K = 1</math>).

Firstly, we will put attention to the fact there are no reactions in the hinged ends, so we also have no shear force in any cross-section of the column. The reason for no reactions can be obtained from [[symmetry]] (so the reactions should be in the same direction) and from moment equilibrium (so the reactions should be in opposite directions).

Using the [[free body diagram]] in the right side of figure 3, and making a summation of moments about point {{mvar|x}}:
<math display="block">\Sigma M = 0  \Rightarrow  M(x) + Pw = 0</math>
where {{mvar|w}} is the lateral deflection.

According to [[Euler–Bernoulli beam theory]], the [[Deflection (engineering)|deflection]] of a beam is related with its [[bending moment]] by:
<math display="block">M = -EI\frac{d^2 w}{dx^2}.</math>

[[File:Pin ended column under the effect of Buckling load.png|thumb|475x475px|''Fig. 3: Pin ended column under the effect of Buckling load'']]
so:
<math display="block">EI\frac{d^2w}{dx^2} + Pw = 0</math>

Let <math>\lambda^2 = \frac{P}{EI}</math>, so:
<math display="block">\frac{d^2w}{dx^2} + \lambda^2 w = 0</math>

We get a classical homogeneous second-order [[ordinary differential equation]].

The general solutions of this equation is: <math>w(x) = A \cos(\lambda x) + B \sin(\lambda x)</math>, where <math>A </math> and <math>B </math> are constants to be determined by [[boundary conditions]], which are:
* Left end pinned: <math> w(0) = 0  \rightarrow  A = 0</math>
* Right end pinned: <math> w(\ell) = 0  \rightarrow  B \sin(\lambda \ell) = 0</math>
[[File:FIG4.png|thumb|355x355px|''Fig. 4: First three modes of buckling loads'']]
If <math>B = 0</math>, no bending moment exists and we get the [[trivial solution]] of <math>w(x) = 0</math>.

However, from the other solution <math>\sin(\lambda \ell) = 0</math> we get <math>\lambda_n \ell = n\pi</math>, for <math>n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots</math>

Together with <math>\lambda^2 = \frac{P}{EI} </math> as defined before, the various critical loads are:
<math display="block">P_{n} = \frac{n^2 \pi^2 EI}{\ell^2} \; , \quad \text{ for } n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots</math>
and depending upon the value of <math>  n </math>, different buckling [[Longitudinal mode|modes]] are produced<ref>{{Cite web| url=http://web.aeromech.usyd.edu.au/AMME2301/Documents/Chapter09.pdf|title=Buckling of Columns|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150528132132/http://web.aeromech.usyd.edu.au/AMME2301/Documents/Chapter09.pdf|archive-date=2015-05-28|url-status=dead}}</ref> as shown in figure 4. The load and mode for n=0 is the nonbuckled mode.

Theoretically, any buckling mode is possible, but in the case of a slowly applied load only the first modal shape is likely to be produced.

'''The critical load of Euler''' for a pin ended column is therefore:  
<math display="block">P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{\ell^2}</math>
and the obtained shape of the buckled column in the first mode is: 
<math display="block">w(x) = B \sin \left({\pi \over \ell} x\right) .</math>

=== General approach ===
[[File:FIG 5.png|thumb|400x400px|''Fig. 5: forces and moments acting on a column.'']]
The differential equation of the axis of a beam<ref>{{Cite book|title=Theory of Elastic Stability |author1=Timoshenko, S. P. |author2=Gere, J. M. | name-list-style=amp | edition = 2 | publisher = McGraw-Hill |year=1961}}</ref> is:
<math display="block">\frac{d^4 w}{dx^4} + \frac{P}{EI}\frac{d^2 w}{dx^2} = \frac{q}{EI}</math>

For a column with axial load only, the lateral load <math>q(x)</math> vanishes and substituting <math>\lambda^2 = \frac{P}{EI}</math>, we get:
<math display="block">\frac{d^4 w}{dx^4} + \lambda^2\frac{d^2 w}{dx^2} = 0</math>

This is a homogeneous fourth-order differential equation and its general solution is
<math display="block">w(x) = A\sin(\lambda x) + B\cos(\lambda x) + Cx + D</math>

The four constants <math>A, B, C, D</math> are determined by the boundary conditions (end constraints) on <math>w(x) </math>, at each end. There are three cases:
# Pinned end:
#: <math>w = 0</math> and <math> M = 0 \rightarrow {d^2w \over dx^2} = 0</math>
# Fixed end:
#: <math>w = 0</math> and <math>{dw \over dx} = 0</math>
# Free end:
#: <math>M = 0 \rightarrow {d^2w \over dx^2} = 0</math> and <math>V = 0 \rightarrow {d^3w \over dx^3} + \lambda^2{dw \over dx} = 0</math>

For each combination of these boundary conditions, an [[eigen value problem|eigenvalue problem]] is obtained. Solving those, we get the values of Euler's critical load for each one of the cases presented in Figure 2.
